title: Fahrenheit 451, Bradbury
subject: litterature
description: In this future, firemen burn books. Guy Montag discovers that culture dies of indifference as much as of censorship.

hero.hook: 451°F: the temperature at which paper catches fire, and at which a society stops thinking.

blocks.text: Published in **1953**, **Fahrenheit 451** is a pillar of the **dystopia**. That genre describes a future society where the individual is crushed. **Ray Bradbury**, born in **1920** and dead in **2012**, imagines a future where firemen burn the books judged dangerous to social stability. The title names the temperature at which paper catches fire, about 233°C.

More than a critique of state censorship, the book shows a population that gives up reading of its own accord, in exchange for empty entertainment and instant technology. Bradbury's warning is simple: freedom of thought is lost through forgetting as much as through force.

sections.title: How a visionary book was born under pressure

blocks.text: The novel grew out of [[McCarthyism]], between **1950** and **1954**. It was a period of anti-communist witch hunts in the United States. Artists and writers were blacklisted. Bradbury adds a nuance: the threat also comes from television and from [[mass consumption]]. Products become standardized and the urge to buy is stimulated without a pause.

blocks.caption: Ray Bradbury, the author who wrote his novel about censorship in a library

blocks.text: Bradbury wrote Fahrenheit 451 in nine days on a typewriter rented in a university library for 10 cents per half hour.

Unlike [[1984]], Orwell's novel where oppression comes from a dictator watching every gesture, here it is the citizens themselves who have given up books. They do it out of comfort and out of fear of argument. Censorship has become a collective choice, not only something imposed.

sections.title: The Montag system: knowledge on fire

blocks.text: **Guy Montag** is a fireman, and his job is to burn illegal libraries. His wife **Mildred** spends her days in front of the **parlors**, screens that cover whole walls. She is absorbed by empty shows. His neighbor **Clarisse** reminds him that firemen once put fires out.

blocks.caption: Burning books: the historical image Bradbury turns into a future dystopia

blocks.text: Montag starts stealing books. His opponent, Captain **Beatty**, knows the classics but burns them with zeal. For him, books create anxiety by exposing inequality and contradiction. Clarisse disappears, probably killed by an automated car. The world has no room left for people who ask questions.

sections.title: Resistance through memory: the book people

blocks.text: Hunted by the **Mechanical Hound**, a police robot, Montag joins a community of intellectuals in exile. Each of them memorizes a whole book to pass it on by voice: Plato's *Republic*, Shakespeare, the Bible. Culture survives in heads, not on paper.
We are books. We have been touched by the fire, but we have survived.

Montag becomes the keeper of **Ecclesiastes**. The novel ends with a nuclear war that destroys the city, but the resisters walk back toward the ruins. Culture can rise from its ashes if humanity agrees to think again.

sections.title: Legacy and a warning about instant everything

blocks.text: Bradbury foresaw flat screens, wireless earpieces, and the [[entertainment society and fragmented attention]]. People are so saturated with fast media that they no longer want to read. In the novel, texts are cut shorter and shorter until they vanish, replaced by quick images.
Bradbury describes radio “seashells” worn in the ear, cutting a person off from the world around them, fifty years before modern wireless earbuds.

There is an irony here: this indictment of censorship was itself cut down in some school editions. The fight for the integrity of the text never ends. **Fahrenheit 451** reminds us that freedom of thought is lost not only by force, but also through forgetting and intellectual laziness.
**Fahrenheit 451** shows that freedom of thought is lost not only by force, but also through forgetting, entertainment, and intellectual laziness.
